title: Home Games

source.quote: the one-time Rescuer changes to an accusing Persecutor instead of a woeful Victim

setting: Rohan and Alisha's marriage runs on more of these than either of them would admit - Sweetheart at parties, Corner when one of them goes quiet instead of answering, Harried when Alisha's to-do list hits six items nobody actually assigned her, Frigid Woman/Man when intimacy itself becomes the battlefield. Tonight it's a dinner party.
playAs: Maya, a friend who keeps getting pulled into the middle of it

L1.line: Isn't she wonderful? Cooks every night - well, except when she burns the rice, ha ha, but we love her anyway!
cues: every eye at the table swings to Alisha, waiting
L1.question: This is Sweetheart - public praise with a needle folded inside it, watching for Alisha's reaction. Which response is the antithesis - the one that doesn't feed the game?

options.text: "I do NOT burn the rice, that happened ONCE."
options.feedback: This gives Rohan exactly what Sweetheart is fishing for - visible irritation that "proves" the jab landed and he was just being playful.

options.text: Say nothing, and go quiet for the rest of the night.
options.feedback: Swallowing it still delivers a payoff - now of private resentment - it just moves the racket feeling off-stage instead of removing it.
Right. Agreeing all the way, with warmth instead of edge, removes the needle's job. There's no gap left between the praise and her reaction for the jab to land in.

options.text: Needle him back publicly about his own flaws.
options.feedback: This escalates into a different game - now you're both Persecuting - it doesn't exit the one already running, it just adds a second one.

L1.lesson: The antithesis isn't about winning the exchange or getting even - that's just playing the game back. It's about declining the specific role the game is built to provoke; for Sweetheart, that means refusing the irritation it's fishing for, not refusing the praise.

L2.intro: Dinner is winding down. Two more rounds are about to start, and you're the one sitting between them.

beats.line: Maya, back me up here - tell Alisha that leaving dishes overnight is disgusting, right?
cues: talking about her in third person while she's sitting right there

options.text: Yeah honestly Alisha, dishes overnight is pretty gross.
options.outcome: Rohan looks triumphant. "SEE? Even Maya agrees." Alisha goes quiet, and the real conversation about dishes never happens.
options.lesson: Delivering a verdict makes you the judge Courtroom needs - the case gets "won," and the actual two people never have to talk to each other.

options.text: I don't really want to referee this one.
options.outcome: Awkward silence. Rohan turns to a different friend to ask the same question.
options.lesson: Opting out is better than ruling, but it still treats this as a case looking for a verdict instead of naming what's actually happening.

options.text: That sounds like something to say to Alisha, not to me - she's right there.
options.outcome: Rohan opens his mouth, closes it, turns to Alisha instead. "...Okay. Alisha, the dishes thing - actually, can we talk about it?"
options.lesson: Refusing to be the third party and redirecting the case back to the two actual parties is the antithesis to Courtroom - no verdict, no judge, no game.

options.text: You two argue about this every week, huh.
options.outcome: Both laugh it off, slightly embarrassed, but still look to you to settle it. "So... who's right?"
options.lesson: Naming the pattern is a good start and stops short of the actual move - it still leaves you holding the gavel if you don't also hand the case back.

beats.line: The kids start full days at school next month... I guess there's nothing stopping me from finishing that degree now.
cues: the obstacle she's complained about for years just disappeared
no excitement in a sentence that's supposed to be about getting her dream back

options.text: That's amazing! You should sign up today!
options.outcome: Alisha's smile is thin. "Yeah... I'll look into it." Three months later, she still hasn't.
options.lesson: Cheering the stated goal takes the social-level words at face value and misses the Switch actually happening in front of you - the obstacle leaving is exactly when If It Weren't For You reveals it was never really about the obstacle.

options.text: You've wanted this for years - what's actually stopping you now?
options.outcome: Long pause. "Honestly? I think I'm scared I'll try and it won't be as good as I imagined." First true sentence in a decade of this complaint.
options.lesson: Naming that the old obstacle is gone and asking what's really in the way catches the Switch cleanly - this is the moment the racketeering ("if it weren't for you") either turns into a real conversation or converts into a full game.

options.text: Well, there's always something, I guess.
options.outcome: "Yeah," Alisha says, visibly relieved. "There's always something." The complaint gets to live on forever.
options.lesson: Agreeing that there's "always something" hands her a replacement obstacle for free - the sympathetic version of this response still protects the game from ever having to resolve.

echo.setting: Four days later. Rohan, mid-story at another gathering, starts winding up for the same kind of toast.
